goal: The user stacks tasks and has an AI work on them, the work resumes once the usage limit lifts, and the results are checked and taken in afterward. Once it's achieved, an AI stacks tasks and lets go, and afterward checks which tasks finished and which were given up, and takes their results in.

deliverable.name: The parts' modules and their interfaces show that they fit together

decisions.decided: The stacker's handoff to the runner carries the queue's start hour and, for each task carried on, the session it had, so the runner needs no read of the record to start.

more.good_when: The developer who writes the runner follows S1 from the stacker's start of the runner to the first task's start, and finds the queue's start hour in what the runner's interfaces take, so the runner can wait until 23:00 as the README's walkthrough says. Today the handoff and `runner.schedule.carry` carry only the queue file's path and the tasks, and `runs.json` keeps no start. The developer who writes `queue.py stack` also finds each way `stacker.stack.stack` refuses, so they can map each one to its exit code. Today `stacker.command.main` gives 2 where the runner can't start, but `stack` names only `Refused`.

The architecture's maker opens the branch and finds the skeleton's list of gaps, with each gap tied to the element it bears on, such as S1's arrow by which the stacker starts the runner with only the queue's tasks and not its start hour. Today the branch holds no `dev/overnight/skeleton-gaps.md`, nor any other list of the skeleton's gaps.
